# 

# 1\. LAB OVERVIEW

## 1.1  Why This Lab Exists

Alert fatigue happens when people receive so many alerts that they stop reacting to them. Its causes are always the same: thresholds below normal behaviour, conditions without a duration (flapping), alerts on causes instead of user symptoms, several rules for the same symptom, critical severity for things that can wait, and alerts without a runbook. The fixes are equally standard: tune thresholds from measured baselines, add "for:", alert on symptoms, de-duplicate rules, use anomaly detection where fixed thresholds do not fit, let Alertmanager group, de-duplicate, route and inhibit notifications, and attach a runbook to every alert.  
In this lab you load the shop's current (noisy) rules, measure one week of alert history, classify each alert, measure baselines and recommend new thresholds, install and unit-test tuned rules including a z-score anomaly alert, configure Alertmanager grouping, de-duplication, routing and inhibition, and prove with a fault that every page arrives grouped and with a working runbook link.

| 🎯  NIIT iRUN Alignment |
| :---- |
| INCIDENT OWNERSHIP: Every page you receive is real, urgent and tells you where to start. |
|  |
| TROUBLESHOOTING EXCELLENCE: Related alerts arrive as one correlated notification instead of a storm. |
|  |
| OPERATIONAL READINESS: Alert rules are tested like code and every alert links to a runbook that exists. |

## 1.3  Conceptual Foundation

Alert hygiene works at two levels: the rules decide when an alert fires, Alertmanager decides who is told, how often and together with what.  
*Figure: Alert Pipeline — Rule (expr \+ for \+ labels \+ runbook\_url) → Prometheus Fires → Alertmanager: De-duplicate (same labels) → Inhibit (cause mutes symptom, critical mutes warning) → Group (team, service) → Route (critical → page, warning → ticket) → Notification With Runbook Link*

| Problem | Symptom in History | Fix in the Rule | Fix in Alertmanager |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Threshold below normal | Fires many times a day, never acted on | Threshold from baseline (p99 \+ margin) | — |
| Flapping | Short alerts (\< 5 min), many fires | for: 2m–10m, longer rate windows | group\_interval, repeat\_interval |
| Duplicate rules | Two alerts always fire together | Delete one, keep the user symptom | Group by service; inhibit |
| No runbook | Responder asks "what now?" | runbook\_url annotation | Show the link in the notification |

*Figure: Threshold vs Anomaly — Fixed Threshold (Error Ratio \> 5 % for 2 min) for Known Limits; z-Score ((x − mean) / stddev \> 3 for 5 min, Baseline Offset 15 min) for Metrics Without a Fixed Limit, Such as Traffic*

* Measure alert noise: volume, flapping, actionability and duplicates

# 3\. CONCEPT DEEP-DIVE BEFORE STARTING

## 3.1  Measure Noise Before You Tune

Alert hygiene starts with data, not opinions. For each alert, count how often it fired (per day), how long it lasted (short alerts that resolve by themselves are flapping), how often someone acknowledged it or opened an incident (actionability), and which other alerts fired at the same time (duplicates or correlation). A healthy pager has few notifications, and nearly all of them are acted on. Alerts that are never acted on are deleted or downgraded to tickets; alerts that always fire together are merged or grouped.

| 💡  Why This Matters Operationally |
| :---- |
| Every non-actionable page trains people to ignore the pager. The real incident then waits in a list of 50 notifications — as in this lab, where four incidents were hidden among 368 alerts. |
|  |
| Tuning is never finished: review the alert report every month and after every incident ("did the right alert fire first, with the right runbook?"). |

## 3.2  The Critical Distinction: Symptoms vs Causes, Thresholds vs Anomalies

Page on symptoms users feel — checkout errors and latency — because they are always worth waking up for; use causes (CPU, pool saturation) for diagnosis, tickets or inhibition. Use a fixed threshold where a clear limit exists (error ratio \> 5 %, p95 \> 1 s). Use anomaly detection — such as a z-score, (current − mean) / standard deviation over a baseline — where "normal" changes and no fixed number fits, for example traffic. Anomaly rules need a baseline that excludes the anomaly itself (offset) and a duration, or they adapt to the problem and stop firing.

| ⚠️  Most Common Mistake With Alerting |
| :---- |
| A team adds HighCPU \> 25 % "to be safe". The checkout service normally runs at 30 %, so the alert fires all day, people mute it — and with it the pager. |
|  |
| REASON: The threshold was chosen without measuring the baseline, and CPU is a cause, not a user symptom. |
|  |
| YOU MUST measure the normal range (quantile\_over\_time) before choosing a threshold, add "for:", and page only on symptoms. |

## 3.3  Alertmanager Settings You Need

| Setting | Does | Lab Value | Effect |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| group\_by | Puts alerts with the same label values into one notification | \[team, service\] | One page per team and service |
| group\_wait / group\_interval | Wait before the first / next notification of a group | 20s / 2m | Related alerts arrive together |
| repeat\_interval | Re-send a still-firing group | 4h | No reminder storm |
| inhibit\_rules | A source alert mutes matching target alerts | critical mutes warning (same service) | Cause or bigger alert first |

| 📝  How to Decide: Delete, Change or Keep |
| :---- |
| Ask: "When this alert fired last week, did someone have to do something urgent?" If never, delete it (or turn it into a dashboard panel or ticket). If sometimes, change it: raise the threshold from the baseline, add a duration, alert on the symptom instead of the cause. If always, keep it — and make sure it has an owner, a severity and a runbook. Alerts that always fire together with another alert are duplicates: keep the one closest to the user. |

| ⌨  Task 1 — Alert history and noise report (\~/day5-lab5) |
| :---- |
|  |
| cat \> work/gen-alert-history.py \<\<'EOF' |
| \#\!/usr/bin/env python3 |
| """Day 5 Lab 5 — writes alert-history.csv: 7 days of alert notifications of the shop (17-23 Oct 2026), seed 7007\. |
| Columns: fired\_at, resolved\_at, alertname, service, severity, duration\_min, acknowledged, incident""" |
| import csv, random |
| from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone |
| random.seed(7007) |
| T0 \= datetime(2026, 10, 17, tzinfo=timezone.utc) |
| rows \= \[\] |
| def add(t, name, svc, sev, dur, ack=False, inc=""): |
|     rows.append(\[t, t \+ timedelta(minutes=dur), name, svc, sev, dur, "yes" if ack else "no", inc\]) |
| def when(): return T0 \+ timedelta(seconds=random.randint(0, 7 \* 86400 \- 3600)) |
| for svc, n in (("checkout", 112), ("frontend", 44)):                      \# CPU above 25 % flaps all week |
|     for \_ in range(n): add(when(), "HighCPU", svc, "critical", random.randint(1, 6)) |
| incidents \= \[(T0 \+ timedelta(days=1, hours=14, minutes=20), "INC-4101", 18), (T0 \+ timedelta(days=3, hours=9, minutes=5), "INC-4117", 25), |
|              (T0 \+ timedelta(days=5, hours=20, minutes=40), "INC-4130", 12)\] |
| for t, inc, dur in incidents:                                            \# three real DB-pool incidents |
|     add(t, "DbPoolSaturated", "inventory", "critical", dur, True, inc) |
|     add(t \+ timedelta(seconds=40), "AnyServerError", "frontend", "critical", dur \- 1, True, inc) |
|     add(t \+ timedelta(seconds=70), "CheckoutSlow", "frontend", "warning", dur \- 2, True, inc) |
|     add(t \+ timedelta(seconds=95), "CheckoutLatencyP95", "checkout", "warning", dur \- 2, False, inc) |
| for \_ in range(81): add(when(), "AnyServerError", "frontend", "critical", random.randint(1, 2))   \# single 5xx responses |
| for \_ in range(59):                                                      \# p95 slightly above 0.2 s, two rules for the same symptom |
|     t, d \= when(), random.randint(2, 15\) |
|     add(t, "CheckoutSlow", "frontend", "warning", d); add(t \+ timedelta(seconds=random.randint(5, 50)), "CheckoutLatencyP95", "checkout", "warning", d) |
| add(T0 \+ timedelta(days=4, hours=2, minutes=12), "ShopSimDown", "shopsim", "critical", 4, True, "INC-4122") |
| rows.sort(key=lambda r: r\[0\]) |
| with open("alert-history.csv", "w", newline="") as f: |
|     w \= csv.writer(f); w.writerow(\["fired\_at", "resolved\_at", "alertname", "service", "severity", "duration\_min", "acknowledged", "incident"\]) |
|     for r in rows: w.writerow(\[r\[0\].strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), r\[1\].strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")\] \+ r\[2:\]) |
| print(f"alert-history.csv: {len(rows)} notifications, {len({r\[7\] for r in rows if r\[7\]})} incidents") |
| EOF |
| cat \> work/alert-noise.py \<\<'EOF' |
| \#\!/usr/bin/env python3 |
| """Day 5 Lab 5 — alert noise report from alert-history.csv: volume, flapping, actionability and duplicates per alert.""" |
| import csv, statistics, sys |
| from collections import defaultdict |
| from datetime import datetime |
| rows \= list(csv.DictReader(open(sys.argv\[1\] if len(sys.argv) \> 1 else "alert-history.csv"))) |
| ts \= lambda s: datetime.strptime(s, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ") |
| by \= defaultdict(list) |
| for r in rows: by\[r\["alertname"\]\].append(r) |
| fires \= {a: sorted(ts(r\["fired\_at"\]) for r in rs) for a, rs in by.items()} |
| def dup\_of(a):                         \# another alert that fires within 2 minutes of \>= 80 % of this alert's notifications |
|     best \= ("", 0.0) |
|     for b in fires: |
|         if b \== a: continue |
|         hit \= sum(any(abs((t \- u).total\_seconds()) \<= 120 for u in fires\[b\]) for t in fires\[a\]) / len(fires\[a\]) |
|         if hit \> best\[1\]: best \= (b, hit) |
|     return f"{best\[0\]} ({best\[1\]:.0%})" if best\[1\] \>= 0.8 else "-" |
| print(f"{'alert':\<20}{'sev':\<9}{'fires':\>6}{'/day':\>6}{'median min':\>11}{'\<5 min':\>8}{'acked':\>7}{'incidents':\>10}  duplicate of") |
| for a, rs in sorted(by.items(), key=lambda kv: \-len(kv\[1\])): |
|     d \= \[int(r\["duration\_min"\]) for r in rs\] |
|     print(f"{a:\<20}{rs\[0\]\['severity'\]:\<9}{len(rs):\>6}{len(rs) / 7:\>6.1f}{statistics.median(d):\>11.0f}{sum(x \< 5 for x in d) / len(d):\>8.0%}" |
|           f"{sum(r\['acknowledged'\] \== 'yes' for r in rs) / len(rs):\>7.0%}{len({r\['incident'\] for r in rs if r\['incident'\]}):\>10}  {dup\_of(a)}") |
| act \= sum(r\["incident"\] \!= "" for r in rows) |
| print(f"\\nTOTAL {len(rows)} notifications in 7 days ({len(rows) / 7:.0f}/day) · linked to an incident: {act} ({act / len(rows):.1%}) · incidents: {len({r\['incident'\] for r in rows if r\['incident'\]})}") |
| EOF |

| alert               sev       fires  /day median min  \<5 min  acked incidents  duplicate of |
| HighCPU             critical    156  22.3          4     67%     0%         0  \- |
| AnyServerError      critical     84  12.0          1     96%     4%         3  \- |
| CheckoutSlow        warning      62   8.9         10     21%     5%         3  CheckoutLatencyP95 (100%) |
| CheckoutLatencyP95  warning      62   8.9         10     21%     0%         3  CheckoutSlow (100%) |

| **1.A  Classify each of the six alerts as DELETE, CHANGE or KEEP and give the evidence (fires/day, \<5 min, acked, duplicate).**   Answer: **HighCPU — DELETE:** 22.3 fires/day, 67% under 5 min (flapping), 0% acked, 0 incidents; it is a non-actionable cause whose threshold (25%) is below normal CPU (\~30%). **AnyServerError — CHANGE:** 12.0 fires/day, 96% under 5 min, 4% acked; fires on single transient 5xx responses, so change it to a 5xx error ratio (\> 5%) with a `for: 2m` duration. **CheckoutSlow — CHANGE:** 8.9 fires/day, 21% under 5 min, 5% acked, 100% duplicate of CheckoutLatencyP95; keep this user-facing symptom rule, raise its threshold from baseline (e.g., \> 0.45s), and add `for: 5m`. **CheckoutLatencyP95 — DELETE:** 8.9 fires/day, 21% under 5 min, 0% acked, 100% duplicate of CheckoutSlow (measures the same checkout latency symptom). **DbPoolSaturated — KEEP:** 0.4 fires/day, 0% under 5 min, 100% acked (3/3 real incidents); genuine critical root-cause alert—ensure it has an owner and `runbook_url`. **ShopSimDown — KEEP:** 0.1 fires/day, 100% acked (1/1 real incident); critical availability alert—ensure it has an owner and `runbook_url`.   |
| **1.B  DbPoolSaturated "fires with" AnyServerError 100 %. Is that a duplicate or a correlation? What should Alertmanager do with it?**  Answer: It is a **correlation (cause-and-effect relationship)**, not a duplicate: database connection pool saturation (`DbPoolSaturated`) causes downstream HTTP 5xx errors (`AnyServerError`). Alertmanager should **group** related alerts by service/team and use **`inhibit_rules`** so the root-cause/critical alert suppresses or correlates with the downstream symptom notification into a single actionable page.   |

| cat \> work/tuned-rules.yml \<\<'EOF' |
| \# Tuned alert rules — symptom-based, with durations, severities, owners and runbooks (Day 5 Lab 5\) |
| groups: |
|   \- name: shop-tuned |
|     rules: |

|         expr: \| |

|         for: 2m |
|         labels: {severity: critical, service: checkout, team: commerce} |
|         annotations: |
|           summary: "Checkout error rate {{ \$value \| humanizePercentage }} (\> 5 % for 2 min)" |
|           runbook\_url: "http\://localhost:9095/runbooks/RB-CHK-002.html" |
|       \- alert: CheckoutLatencyHigh |
|         expr: \| |
|           histogram\_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http\_server\_request\_duration\_seconds\_bucket{env="lab",service="frontend",route="/api/checkout"}\[5m\]))) \> 1 |
|         for: 5m |
|         labels: {severity: warning, service: checkout, team: commerce} |

| **2.A  Write your threshold recommendation for each noisy rule (new expression or DELETE, for:, severity) and the baseline value that justifies it.**   Answer: HighCPU: DELETE — Normal p99 CPU baselines are \~0.35 (checkout) and \~0.27 (frontend), exceeding the 0.25 threshold continuously; CPU is an internal cause, not a user-facing symptom. \| AnyServerError: REPLACE with CheckoutErrorRateHigh (5xx error ratio \> 0.05, for: 2m, severity: critical) to avoid paging on single transient 5xx responses. \| CheckoutSlow: REPLACE with CheckoutLatencyHigh (p95 \> 1s, for: 5m, severity: warning) because the healthy p95 baseline is \~0.24–0.25s. \| CheckoutLatencyP95: DELETE — 100% duplicate of CheckoutSlow measuring the same checkout latency symptom. |
| **2.B  Why does the anomaly rule compare with the hour that ended 15 minutes ago (offset 15m) instead of the last hour?**   Answer: Using offset 15m excludes the most recent 15 minutes (including the active incident and the 5m evaluation window) from the 1-hour baseline window. Without this offset, an ongoing traffic drop or spike would skew the rolling mean and inflate the standard deviation, shrinking the z-score and causing the alert to self-resolve prematurely while the anomaly is still happening.  |

| TASK 3 — GROUP & DE-DUPLICATE: Alertmanager Routing, Grouping and Inhibition |
| :---- |

| 3 | Group, De-duplicate and Inhibit Notifications*Alert Hygiene & Correlation SOP — Day 5 — Lab 5* | ⏱ 7 min |
| :---: | :---- | :---: |

The kit contains a webhook sink that prints every notification and serves runbooks; you replace the starting Alertmanager configuration with one that groups by team and service, pages for critical and creates tickets for warnings, and inhibits warnings while a critical alert of the same service fires. With amtool you send the same alert three times, a second alert and a warning, and watch what arrives.

| ⌨  Task 3 — Alertmanager configuration (\~/day5-lab5) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# The webhook sink (webhook-sink.py) and the runbook folder are part of the kit and already run: docker compose ps webhook-sink |
| cp alertmanager/alertmanager.yml work/alertmanager-day1.yml ![][image19] |
| cat \> alertmanager/alertmanager.yml \<\<'EOF' |
| \# Alertmanager — Day 5 Lab 5: grouping, de-duplication, routing by severity, inhibition, runbook links |
| route: |
|   receiver: oncall-page |
|   group\_by: \[team, service\]          \# one notification per team and service, however many alerts fire |
|   group\_wait: 20s                    \# wait for related alerts before the first notification |
|   group\_interval: 2m                 \# new alerts in an existing group are sent at most every 2 minutes |
|   repeat\_interval: 4h                \# a still-firing group is re-sent after 4 hours, not every few minutes |
|   routes: |
|     \- matchers: \[severity="warning"\] |
|       receiver: team-ticket          \# warnings create a ticket, they do not page |
| receivers: |
|   \- name: oncall-page |
|     webhook\_configs: \[{url: "http\://webhook-sink:9095/page", send\_resolved: true}\] |
|   \- name: team-ticket |
|     webhook\_configs: \[{url: "http\://webhook-sink:9095/ticket", send\_resolved: false}\] |
| inhibit\_rules: |
|   \- source\_matchers: \[severity="critical"\]          \# a critical alert mutes warnings of the same service |
|     target\_matchers: \[severity="warning"\] |
|     equal: \[service\] |
|   \- source\_matchers: \[alertname="InventoryDbPoolSaturated"\]   \# the known cause mutes its latency symptom |
|     target\_matchers: \[alertname="CheckoutLatencyHigh"\] |
| EOF ![][image20] |
| docker compose exec \-T alertmanager amtool check-config /etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml && curl \-s \-X POST localhost:9093/-/reload ![][image21] |
| docker compose exec \-T alertmanager amtool config routes test \--config.file=/etc/alertmanager/alertmanager.yml severity=warning team=commerce ![][image22] |

| team-ticket |

| docker compose exec \-T alertmanager amtool \--alertmanager.url=http\://localhost:9093 alert add alertname=PaymentErrorsTest service=payment team=commerce severity=critical \--annotation=runbook\_url=[http\://localhost:9095/runbooks/RB-CHK-002.html](http://localhost:9095/runbooks/RB-CHK-002.html) ![][image24] |
| docker compose exec \-T alertmanager amtool \--alertmanager.url=http\://localhost:9093 alert add alertname=PaymentQueueTest service=payment team=commerce severity=warning ![][image25] |
| docker compose exec \-T alertmanager amtool \--alertmanager.url=http\://localhost:9093 alert query alertname=\~"Payment.\*Test" ![][image26] |
| docker compose exec \-T alertmanager amtool \--alertmanager.url=http\://localhost:9093 alert query \--inhibited alertname=PaymentQueueTest ![][image27] |

| **📟  Expected Output** |
| Alertname           Starts At   Summary  State |
| PaymentLatencyTest  …           copy-3   active     ← three adds, ONE alert (same labels) |
| PaymentErrorsTest   …                    active     (PaymentQueueTest not listed: suppressed) |
| PaymentQueueTest    …                    suppressed |
| /page    FIRING   group={"service": "payment", "team": "commerce"} alerts=2 |
|          \- PaymentErrorsTest \[critical\] payment  runbook=http\://localhost:9095/runbooks/RB-CHK-002.html |
|          \- PaymentLatencyTest \[critical\] payment  runbook=http\://localhost:9095/runbooks/RB-CHK-002.html |
| **3.A  Five amtool commands produced one notification with two alerts. Explain which step was de-duplication, which grouping and which inhibition.**   Answer: De-duplication: The loop that executed three alert add commands for PaymentLatencyTest with identical label sets (alertname, service, team, severity) collapsed all three into a single active alert (keeping the latest summary=copy-3). \| Grouping: Alertmanager batched the two distinct critical alerts for the same service (PaymentLatencyTest and PaymentErrorsTest) together under group\_by: \[team, service\] into a single /page notification containing alerts=2. \| Inhibition: The inhibit\_rules rule matched the active critical alerts on service=payment and suppressed the lower-severity PaymentQueueTest (severity=warning) alert on the same service so no separate ticket notification was sent. |
| **3.B  Why is group\_by \[team, service\] better than grouping by alertname for an on-call engineer?**  Answer: Grouping by \[team, service\] consolidates all related symptoms for an impacted service (such as both latency and errors on the payment service) into a single incident page routed to the owning team, giving the on-call engineer full incident context at once instead of flooding them with separate pages per alert rule during the same outage.  |

# 6\. TROUBLESHOOTING — COMMON ISSUES & FIXES

| Issue / Error | Cause | Diagnosis | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| promtool test: FAILED … got: \[\] | Rule expression or for: changed | Read exp vs got in the output | Keep the test file in step with the rules |
| Rules not loaded after reload | File not in prometheus/rules or YAML error | docker compose exec \-T prometheus promtool check rules … | Fix YAML; file must be prometheus/rules/\*.yml |
| Duplicate alert names after Task 2 | Baseline alerts.yml still in rules/ | ls prometheus/rules/ | Move alerts.yml to work/ |
| webhook-sink not reachable from Alertmanager | Container stopped or port 9095 in use | docker compose ps webhook-sink; docker compose logs webhook-sink | docker compose up \-d webhook-sink; free port 9095 |
| amtool: label parsing warning | Unquoted values with spaces | Read the suggestion in the warning | Use values without spaces or quote them |
| No page during the fault | group\_wait/for: not yet reached | Check Prometheus Alerts page: pending? | Wait the full 4 minutes |

# 7\. INSTRUCTOR DEBRIEF — 7 MINUTES

## 7.1  Discussion Questions

| Discussion 1 — 3.5 % Actionable |
| :---- |
| Which single change removes the most notifications from last week? |
| Who should approve deleting an alert? |
|  |
| Key insight: deleting HighCPU and the duplicate rule removes \~60 % of the noise; the service owner and on-call agree on deletions. |
| **Discussion 2 — Thresholds From Data** |
| Why is "p99 of the healthy baseline \+ margin" a better starting point than a round number? |
| When must thresholds be reviewed again? |
|  |
| Key answer: it is just above normal behaviour by definition; review after capacity changes, releases and every incident. |
| **Discussion 3 — Anomaly Detection** |
| When is a z-score better than a fixed threshold, and when is it worse? |
| What happens to a z-score alert on a quiet night or during a sale? |
|  |
| Answer: good for metrics without a fixed limit; bad for seasonal patterns — compare with the same time last week (offset 1w) or use longer baselines. |
| **Discussion 4 — Correlation** |
| The fault produced two pages for two teams. Should it be one? |
| How would an incident tool correlate them further (same time, dependency map)? |
|  |
| Key answer: two owners need two pages; correlation tools link them into one incident using time and topology — the runbooks point to each other. |

## 7.2  Common Mistakes — Learn From These

| Mistake | Why It Happens | Consequence | Prevention |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Round-number thresholds | Feels safe | Fires on normal behaviour | Measure baseline first |
| No for: | Fast alerts wanted | Flapping | for: 2m–10m |
| Paging on causes | CPU looks important | Non-actionable pages | Page on symptoms; causes for tickets/inhibition |
| Untested rules | YAML looks right | Silent failures | promtool check \+ test in CI |
| Runbook "TBD" | Written later | Responder lost | runbook\_url required and link-checked |

# 8\. EXTENSION TASKS (Advanced Learners)

| Extension A — Weekly Seasonality |
| :---- |
| Change the anomaly baseline to the same time last week (offset 1w). |
| Which problems does that solve, and which new ones does it create? |
| Key question: how much history do you need? **Updated PromQL Expression (`offset 1w`):** Code snippet `abs(   (sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{env="lab",service="frontend"}[5m]))     - avg_over_time(sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{env="lab",service="frontend"}[5m]))[1h:1m] offset 1w))   / stddev_over_time(sum(rate(http_server_requests_total{env="lab",service="frontend"}[5m]))[1h:1m] offset 1w) ) > 3`  **Which problems does that solve?**It eliminates false positives caused by normal daily and weekly traffic cycles (e.g., Monday morning login spikes, weekend traffic drops, or scheduled weekly batch jobs) because current traffic is compared against the exact same day of the week and hour rather than the preceding hour. **Which new problems does it create? Holiday & promotional distortion:** Public holidays, flash sales, or major marketing campaigns either last week or this week will skew the comparison and trigger false alerts. **Baseline contamination:** If there was a major outage at that exact time last week, the historical mean/stddev will be corrupted, potentially masking a real drop this week. **Organic growth drift:** Rapid week-over-week user growth or a new feature launch can gradually push normal traffic past 3 standard deviations. **Key question — How much history do you need?**You need **at least 7 days plus 1 hour** of continuous Prometheus TSDB retention (`--storage.tsdb.retention.time` greater than `7d1h`, practically 14–15 days so a single week-old outage doesn't leave you blind, or 4 weeks if averaging across multiple weeks).  |
| **Extension B — Silence for Maintenance** |
| Create a silence with docker compose exec \-T alertmanager amtool \--alertmanager.url=http\://localhost:9093 silence add service=checkout \--duration=30m \--comment="maintenance". |
| Run the fault again — what reaches the sink? |
| Compare silences with inhibition. **Commands to run the maintenance silence & fault test:** Bash `docker compose exec -T alertmanager amtool --alertmanager.url=http://localhost:9093 silence add service=checkout --duration=30m --comment="maintenance" echo db-pool > control/fault; sleep 240 docker compose logs --no-log-prefix --since 4m webhook-sink | grep -vi payment echo none > control/fault`  **What reaches the sink?Only `InventoryDbPoolSaturated`** (`group={"service": "inventory", "team": "catalog"}`) reaches `/page` on `webhook-sink`. `CheckoutErrorRateHigh` (`service="checkout"`) still fires in Prometheus and appears as `suppressed` in Alertmanager, so it is blocked from reaching the sink. **Compare silences with inhibition: Silences** are **manual, time-bound overrides** (`startsAt` to `endsAt`) created by an operator for planned maintenance or known issues; they suppress matching alerts unconditionally regardless of whether any other alert is firing. **Inhibition** is **dynamic, event-driven suppression** defined in `alertmanager.yml`; a target alert is suppressed *only while* a higher-priority source alert (e.g., `severity="critical"` on the same `service`) is actively firing, and automatically un-suppresses the moment the source alert resolves.  |
| **Extension C — Rules in CI** |
| Write a CI step that runs promtool check rules, promtool test rules and the link check. |
| Fail the build if any alert lacks runbook\_url or for:. |
| Where would you run it in your pipeline?  **CI Step Script (Shell / GitHub Actions / GitLab CI):** Bash `#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail RULE_FILE="prometheus/rules/tuned-rules.yml" TEST_FILE="work/tuned-rules.test.yml" # 1. Lint syntax and check rule validity promtool check rules "$RULE_FILE" # 2. Run unit tests (copy test file alongside rule_files target) cp "$TEST_FILE" prometheus/rules/ promtool test rules prometheus/rules/tuned-rules.test.yml rm -f prometheus/rules/tuned-rules.test.yml # 3. Fail build if any alerting rule lacks 'for:' or 'annotations.runbook_url' python3 - "$RULE_FILE" <<'PY' import sys, yaml data = yaml.safe_load(open(sys.argv[1])) errors = [] for group in data.get("groups", []):     for rule in group.get("rules", []):         if "alert" not in rule:             continue         name = rule["alert"]         if not rule.get("for"):             errors.append(f"{name}: missing 'for:' duration")         url = rule.get("annotations", {}).get("runbook_url", "")         if not url or "TBD" in url:             errors.append(f"{name}: missing or placeholder 'runbook_url'") if errors:     print("Alert hygiene check failed:\n - " + "\n - ".join(errors))     sys.exit(1) print("Alert hygiene check passed: all alerts have 'for:' and valid 'runbook_url'.") PY # 4. Verify runbook links are reachable (when runbook server is up or against local files) grep -oE 'http://localhost:9095/runbooks/[^" ]+' "$RULE_FILE" | sort -u | while read -r url; do     curl -fsS -o /dev/null "$url" || { echo "Broken runbook link: $url"; exit 1; } done`  **Where would you run it in your pipeline?**Run the static checks (`promtool check rules`, `promtool test rules`, the YAML policy check for `for:` / `runbook_url`, and local runbook file existence checks) on **every Pull Request / Merge Request** as a required pre-merge gate, and run the live HTTP link check (`curl`) in the **staging/post-deploy verification stage** right before reloading Prometheus in production.  |

# 10\. QUICK REFERENCE — ALERT HYGIENE & CORRELATION COMMAND CARD

Bookmark this page. Every command you need in SOP order.

| Category | Command | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Baseline | quantile\_over\_time(0.99, metric\[30m\]) | Normal range |
| Time above threshold | avg\_over\_time((metric \> bool 0.25)\[30m:5s\]) | Share of time |
| Duration | for: 2m | No flapping |
| Symptom alert | error ratio \> 0.05 · p95 \> 1 s | Page |
| z-score | abs((x \- avg\_over\_time(x\[1h:1m\] offset 15m)) / stddev\_over\_time(…)) \> 3 | Anomaly |
| Unit test | promtool test rules rules.test.yml | Rules as code |
| Group | group\_by: \[team, service\] | One page per owner |
| Timing | group\_wait 20s · group\_interval 2m · repeat\_interval 4h | Fewer notifications |
| Route | matchers: \[severity="warning"\] → ticket | Page vs ticket |
| Inhibit | source critical → target warning, equal: \[service\] | Mute symptoms |
| Test routing | amtool config routes test … labels | Which receiver |
| Runbook | annotations: runbook\_url: http\://… | Link check 200 |

# APPENDIX A — INSTRUCTOR PRE-CLASS RUNBOOK (INSTRUCTOR ONLY)

INSTRUCTOR ONLY — this lab needs no cloud account and no other lab. Each learner runs the kit on their own laptop (Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with Compose v2) or on a personal VM (2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM is plenty; about 400 MB RAM per stack).  
1\. Distribute lab5-kit.zip one day before. Images pulled once: prom/prometheus:v3.5.0, prom/alertmanager:v0.28.1, python:3.12-slim (about 400 MB). For a locked-down network export them with docker save and share the tar file.  
2\. The kit binds ports 9090, 9093 and 9095 to 127.0.0.1. On a VM set BIND=0.0.0.0 in .env and open the ports only to the learner's own IP. Alertmanager and the webhook sink have no authentication.

| ⌨  Instructor — kit self-test (run once before class) |
| :---- |
|  |
| \# 1\. Start and verify (all lines OK; no alert firing) |
| cd \~/day5-lab5 && ./scripts/setup.sh |
| \# 2\. Dry run of the solution files (a working copy of the whole lab, about 3 minutes) |
| cp solutions/tuned-rules.yml solutions/tuned-rules.test.yml prometheus/rules/ |
| docker compose exec \-T \-w /etc/prometheus/rules prometheus promtool test rules tuned-rules.test.yml |
| cp solutions/alertmanager.yml alertmanager/alertmanager.yml && cp solutions/RB-WEB-004.html runbooks/ && curl \-s \-X POST localhost:9093/-/reload |
| \# 3\. Back to the starting state (removes tuned rules, restores the starting Alertmanager configuration and runbooks you added) |
| rm \-f runbooks/RB-WEB-004.html; ./scripts/reset.sh |

3\. Alert history: alert-history.csv in work/ is generated with a fixed seed (7007); every learner sees the same 368 notifications, 3.5 % linked to incidents. Prometheus evaluation interval is 5 s and the retention 6 h, so the end-to-end fault test (Task 4, about 4 minutes) produces its pages reliably; expected timings can differ by about 30 seconds.  
4\. Unverified on your platform: the exact promtool unit-test output, the Alertmanager 0.28 amtool route output and the expected z-score value depend on image versions. Run the self-test once and adjust the expected-output lines in the guide if your versions differ. Clean-up: docker compose down \-v; delete the folder.
